pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Go has no try/catch. How does a Go function tell its caller something went wrong, and what do Gophers like about that compared to exceptions?
expected_points: a fallible function returns an error as an ordinary value, by convention the last return value
nil means success; non-nil carries a failure description
no hidden control flow — every place a failure can happen is visible in the code
errors obey normal value rules: return, store, compare, pass along

questions.prompt: Describe the standard shape of calling a function that can fail. What do you do when err is non-nil, and what about the other return value?
expected_points: value, err := f() then if err != nil immediately after the call
if you cannot handle it, return the error (plus a zero value) to your caller
never use the other return value when err is non-nil — it is a meaningless zero value
error branches return early so the happy path stays unindented

questions.prompt: fmt.Errorf("transfer: %w", err) versus fmt.Errorf("transfer: %v", err) — the printed messages are identical. What is the difference and why does it matter?
expected_points: %w keeps the original error inside the new one, forming a chain
errors.Is can still find the underlying sentinel through the chain
%v flattens the error to text, severing the chain so errors.Is returns false

questions.prompt: In the exercise, why is ErrInsufficientFunds a package-level variable instead of fmt.Errorf("insufficient funds") at the failure site? When is the ad-hoc form the right call?
expected_points: a sentinel is one identity callers can branch on with errors.Is
matching message text is brittle — wording changes and wrapping break it
ad-hoc errors are right when the message is only for humans and no caller branches on it

questions.prompt: A failed transfer prints: transfer from "alice" to "bob": withdraw 100 from "alice": have 50: insufficient funds. How was that message built, and what can code still learn from the error beyond reading the text?
expected_points: each layer wrapped the error it received with fmt.Errorf and %w, adding its own context
fragments read outermost first, which is why messages are lowercase without trailing punctuation
errors.Is(err, ErrInsufficientFunds) is still true — the cause survives every layer

questions.prompt: err == ErrAccountNotFound compiles and sometimes even works. Why is it still the wrong way to check?
expected_points: == compares only the outermost error
it silently becomes false as soon as any layer wraps the sentinel
errors.Is walks the whole chain, so it keeps working as the code evolves

questions.prompt: Why does Go convention say error messages should be lowercase with no trailing punctuation?
expected_points: messages get chained with a colon separator as errors are wrapped
capitalized or punctuated fragments read badly in the middle of a chain
